definition: Private Intelligence is OpenAI's confidential AI offering announced at DevDay 2026: AI processing with zero data retention. When your data goes in — prompts, documents, tool outputs — none of it is kept afterward. It pairs that with automated safety review, so the system is still checked for misuse without a human reading your content. It's aimed at enterprises handling sensitive material — health, finance, legal — that couldn't otherwise touch a cloud AI. A confidential inference preview was promised for fall 2026; enterprise access is by contacting OpenAI, and pricing wasn't published.

edges.label: the trust side of access
edges.note: MCP restrictions govern what the AI may touch; Private Intelligence governs what happens to what it saw.

edges.label: lets regulated industries deploy agents
edges.note: Zero-retention inference removes the data-leakage objection that kept AI out of hospitals and banks.

example.body: A hospital wants to summarize patient discharge notes with AI — but patient data can't be stored on outside servers. With zero data retention, the notes are processed and the system keeps nothing: no logs of the content, no training on the text. The automated safety review still runs to catch misuse, but the data itself is gone the moment the answer comes back. The AI forgets everything by design.

footnotes.body: “Zero data retention” is OpenAI's claim, paired with automated safety review. For regulated use (health, finance, legal), verify the claim against your own compliance requirements rather than taking a keynote slide as proof — the details of what is reviewed, logged, and attested matter.
footnotes.label: Caveat: verify the claim

name: Private Intelligence
tagline: Confidential AI with zero data retention: your data goes in, nothing stays behind.
whyItMatters: The number-one reason companies ban AI tools is data leakage. Zero-retention inference removes that objection. If it works as advertised, it moves AI from “that fun tool we can't use at work” to infrastructure that regulated industries can actually adopt — which is where the serious agent deployments will happen.
